newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: OPINION - Offshore rates niggle RBNZ's balancing act.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - Offshore rates niggle RBNZ's balancing act.

text.p: By Stephen Roberts, International Economist, UBS Australia.
SYDNEY, Nov 1 - The Reserve Bank of New Zealand seems to have started the monetary policy easing process earlier than we had previously expected.

Less than a fortnight after declaring that the good CPI reading meant no immediate change in monetary conditions, the RBNZ said the recent appreciation of the currency meant that overall monetary conditions, even after allowing for the small dip in short term interest rates, had tightened more than was necessary for the policy purpose of achieving the 0-2 percent inflation target.

The RBNZ is now trying to rebalance monetary conditions, and that means settling for somewhat lower short term interest rates than it would like in order to achieve a currency that is not too much stronger than it would like.

This policy balancing act is going to be all the more precarious because it is being partly driven by forces over which the RBNZ has no control at all -- very low yields in countries such as Japan driving footloose international capital to seek out high yields.

Also, settling for a lower short term interest rate structure than the RBNZ would like is relatively risky in an environment where fiscal policy has already been eased and is likely to be eased further under whatever government eventuates from the current coalition discussions.
The risks associated with the current monetary policy balancing act aimed at containing the New Zealand dollar are more on the 1998, rather than the 1997 horizon.

Very tight monetary conditions through 1995 and 1996 will still generate subdued economic growth and very low inflation through 1997. But 1998 may well see the start of a significant rebound in economic growth.
SHORT TERM INTEREST RATE OUTLOOK

The outlook for short term interest rates has become more complex and is now dependent on the extent of any recovery in the New Zealand dollar and how much discreet monetary policy easing the RBNZ feels is warranted in 1997.
We see the first staging post for the 90 day bank bill yield being around nine percent.

A nine percent 90 day bank bill yield combined with the New Zealand dollar around $US0.7000 and a Trade Weighted Index above about 66.5 would be broadly consistent with the monetary policy assumptions in the September Economic Forecasts of a 90 day bank bill yield around 10 percent with a 65 TWI.

It would also be consistent with both of the RBNZ's recent statements implying no change in overall monetary conditions required for policy purposes but a preference to rebalance excessive currency strength against somewhat lower interest rates.

One problem with the new balance of monetary conditions is that nine percent short term interest rates are still high enough to cause the currency to drift up again and another "rebalancing" statement from the RBNZ over the coming months cannot be ruled out.
Also, the RBNZ is likely to reassess monetary policy settings in the December 17 Monetary Policy Statement.

We still see the December quarter CPI release on January 17 being the critical determinant of how comfortable the RBNZ will be with a discreet policy easing. Policy easing, in the New Zealand context, means a lower benchmark for both the TWI and
short term interest rates.
We would see the first discreet easing being cautious and small, given the likely fiscal expansion in train and the risk of very strong economic growth rebound in late 1997 and in 1998.
Our 1997 target for short term interest rates remains around eight percent, but with the risk to the down-side if the New Zealand dollar stays strong.
LONG TERM INTEREST RATE OUTLOOK
Short term interest rates are starting to step down, a process that will continue either because of renewed currency strength or an easing in overall monetary conditions in 1997.
New Zealand's inflation rate is also on it way down, responding to very tight monetary conditions over the past two years.
Annual inflation is likely to fall below one percent during 1997.
The government's budget will stay in very solid surplus for the foreseeable future, regardless of the government that emerges from current coalition discussions.

Will real yields at the long end of the curve need to be straining six percent during 1997? The answer is almost certainly no and even five percent would be a pretty high yield in the softish economic conditions likely during much of 1997.
That means the New Zealand 10 year bond yield has potential to push well below seven percent over the next 12 months and possibly sub 6.5 percent.
YIELD CURVE OUTLOOK
Even though the 90 day bank bill has come down, it has not come down very far. As a result, the "L" shaped yield curve stays in place but with the base shifting down to around seven percent.
Once it becomes clearer that the RBNZ is moving towards generally easier monetary conditions, the base of the "L" will tip to a more positive shape from 1998 out.
Expectations of easier monetary conditions are likely to have most pronounced impact on the middle past of the curve, particularly the 2000-2002 part of the curve.
NEW ZEALAND DOLLAR OUTLOOK
Monetary policy requirements have changed.

Rather than holding 90 day bank bill yield up at 9.5 percent, regardless of the implications for the New Zealand dollar as we had preciously thought was the Reserve Bank's policy intention, the bank has moved to offset currency strength with lower short term interest rates.

The reduction in the 90 day bank bill yield is relatively small at this stage but implies the New Zealand dollar centring around $US0.7000 at end 1995 and with appreciation potential on what will still be a relatively high yield structure to a peak of 0.7100 over the next 12 months.
Whenever the currency approaches 0.7100, or more than about 67.5 on the TWI Basis, the risk will be on the side of the RBNZ allowing short term interests rates to edge down.
By the second half of 1997, the RBNZ is likely to focus on potentially much stronger economic growth in 1998 and the associated risk of rising inflationary pressures.
By late 1997 the RBNZ is likely to allow the overall bias in monetary conditions to tighten again.
(Note - The opinions expressed in this article represent the views of the author only. They should not be seen as reflecting the views of Reuters.)
